## What has been tried

Newest first. The `why` is the part that will still be worth reading later.

**2026-08-24T19:10:07Z** — lease stand-down rehearsal against a live supervisor · *MEASURED*

- config: `a real supervisor with a real worker, told its lease ends in 31 minutes with a 30-minute stand-down lead`
- produced: it ran normally for 60 s, entered the lead window at exactly expiry-minus-30m, stopped the worker, banked, verified every file's md5 against the commit, and retired the box in the registry
- why: The unit test covers the decision; this covers the plumbing, and they are different claims. The 18-hour lease cap makes this the most-used path in the whole system over a month, and it is the one path where getting it wrong destroys a box's work rather than merely stopping it.
- control: it did NOT stand down during the first minute, when the deadline was 31 minutes out — a stand-down that fires immediately whatever you tell it would pass the same test

**2026-08-24T19:08:37Z** — banking through a third-party push to main · *MEASURED*

- config: `bank now runs git fetch + rebase when the branch has diverged, retries the push, and forces only the render box's scratch ref`
- produced: origin/main == local HEAD at 6e113c1e, with the other session's 992c438 an ancestor of ours; three banks in a row before the fix recorded PUSH FAILED while the mirror kept succeeding
- why: This repo is not ours alone and a months-long system must survive its colleagues. The failure was also instructive about layering: the mirror and the push have no credential, service or machine in common, which is exactly why one kept working while the other was broken for twelve minutes.
- control: a test builds a bare origin and two clones, has the second push first, and requires the rebase to keep BOTH pieces of work; the same test then requires sync to be a no-op when nothing is upstream

**2026-08-24T19:01:04Z** — the recovery demonstration: kill -9 mid-flight, wipe the box, continue from the repo · *MEASURED*

- config: `kill -9 on supervisor and worker (no run_stop, no final bank), rm -rf the checkout and the harness state on the box, then a clean clone + build + tmhaul recover + tmhaul watch --detach`
- produced: detected from the repo alone as CRITICAL zero_throughput 12m after the last sample; recovered with resume_evals=80 read out of the repo; throughput resumed 80 -> 160 -> 189 evals and every alarm cleared. Cost of the crash: 34 evals, about 90 seconds. Clone 3.8 s, build 4.9 s.
- why: This is the deliverable that proves the rest. Durability claims are cheap to write and this project has been burned by exactly that; the only convincing form is to destroy the box and show the work continue. It also produced the honest bound: a crash costs at most one banking window of RECORD, and artifacts survive only if the worker writes them into state/frontier -- which the rung-1 explorer will have to do and the sweep did not need to.
- control: the same fresh checkout, 1m34s after the kill, fired NOTHING — so the alarm is capable of silence, which is the half that makes the firing mean something. And the mirror's 17 files came back byte-identical to the clone's: two transports (GitHub via a deploy key on Windows, a paste via x509) with nothing in common, agreeing.

**2026-08-24T18:44:33Z** — pushing to GitHub from an on-demand box · *MEASURED*

- config: `git bundle -> wsx (md5 both ends) -> WhiteStick's ~/haul-push clone -> deploy key -> origin/main`
- produced: commit 409eb2c6 and 28c92363 both on origin/main; git ls-remote agrees with local HEAD
- why: The brief requires the repo to be the state of record, pushed continuously. No OD holds a GitHub credential, which reads as impossible; it is not, it is a 161-byte navi credential file away. Recording the route here because the next session will hit the same wall.
- control: the push driver refuses to report success unless the sha the render box pushed equals our own HEAD, so a bundle that carried the wrong thing is an error rather than a green line

**2026-08-24T18:44:33Z** — the standing re-simulation sweep as the harness's first real workload · *MEASURED*

- config: `tmresim --loop --pause-s 300, plain oracle in process via ghost::oracle::validate_many, batched one server launch per map`
- produced: 7 of 7 tapes on Kacky Reloaded #290 re-simulated at exactly their published times in 6 s; the full sweep is 174 tapes across 36 maps
- why: The project's rule is that a banked result is re-simulated by the plain oracle standing, not as a spot check — and until now nothing made that true. It is also the right first job for the harness: hours long, countable, real failure modes, and it reads a corpus that is NOT in the repo, which is what surfaced the one real gap in the recovery story.
- control: the no-ghost gate is two-sided and tested: a human recording is refused, one of our own tapes is accepted, and a file nothing places is refused rather than assumed ours

**2026-08-24T18:44:33Z** — the long-haul harness itself · *MEASURED*

- config: `tmhaul: repo-as-state-of-record, detached supervisor, cron heartbeat, 8 alarms, work-counting budget; tmresim as the first worker`
- produced: 86 + 12 tests green; every alarm fired from a fixture and against a live process; a full bank does commit + paste mirror + GitHub push in about 70 s
- why: Every failure the project hit on 2026-08-24 was a durability failure, not an algorithm failure. The five were: a supervising agent settling while its child ran; a stall detector that could not fire at zero evals; the 18-hour lease cap; a 30-day store used as a months-long one; and a budget clock burning during a stall. Each is answered by a mechanism rather than a note in a document, because a note does not fire at 3am.
- control: alarms selftest pairs each alarm with a state that must fire it AND a healthy control that must fire nothing; live-test runs four real workers (normal, stall, crash, silent) and reads the firings back off disk
